name: Uma Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We do not sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and have handled water-service calls and chats at a contact centre for years, at about the team's ordinary pace. I finished secondary school and work evenings for a higher rate; I have never used AI and keep a ruled paper book of promised restoration times. I like calling a household back with a real update, and I dislike a vague answer that leaves them waiting with no water.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the new reply button may save a minute, but the water account still needs a proper check. A household should not be told its supply is restored because a screen guessed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used AI and do not need to try it for a small change. My evening rota pays well and we have ten months of expenses saved, so I expect to keep working while we pay the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the evening service calls and record every promised restoration time in my paper handover book. During the first year of this plateau, I'd add part of each pay to savings and ask for a written procedure if the reply button becomes compulsory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A busy outage night is tiring enough without treating every new button as a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the paper book prevent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A caller once rang back after an estimated water time changed, and the handover book showed who promised the first time. I found the updated notice and rang her myself before another agent guessed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask for writing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a tool sends a wrong restoration time, I want to know who corrects it and what we tell the customer. A written rule for wrong water-restoration times gives every call shift the same answer.

S0.quote: A written rule for wrong water-restoration times gives every call shift the same answer.
say: I would check the **water account** before trusting a quick reply.
I would avoid giving a **guessed restoration time** to households.
think: I have never used AI and see no need for it in a **small change**.
I have **ten months** saved and a higher evening rate, so the mortgage feels covered.
do: Keep **evening service calls** and record promised times in the handover book.
Add part of each **pay packet** to savings.
Ask for a **written procedure** if the new button becomes compulsory.
fieldNote: Uma uses a **paper handover book** to trace a changed restoration time across shifts.
Her **ten-month reserve** and evening premium make the mild scenario feel secure.

steps.text: Keep evening utility calls and record promised times in the paper handover book
Add part of each pay packet to savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the manager for the evening roster before agreeing that faster replies are good news. Standard outage questions may go to software, but the person with no water will still expect someone to answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know routine calls fill much of my shift. I could lose my evening call premium without losing my contact-centre job title. Ten months saved helps us look around, but a new centre's daytime wage may not cover our mortgage and two children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a paper count of callbacks and compare it with the paid evening rota each month. If the new tool becomes required, I'd practise on closed outage cases with a supervisor; in its first year, if my hours fall, I'd apply for a posted paid utility desk job nearby only if its written wage and hours cover our bills, and I would keep this shift until I sign an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I know where the current screen hides an outage note; I do not want a shorter pay packet while I learn another.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should supervised practice look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want a false restoration time on a test account and a way to correct it. If I cannot undo a mistake in practice, I will not send the first live reply alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if only daytime jobs are posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the whole week's pay, not the title. My partner Tomas and I agreed the mortgage comes before a neat daytime schedule.

S1.quote: I could lose my evening call premium without losing my contact-centre job title.
say: I would ask for the **paid evening roster** before praising faster replies.
I would insist a person answers **urgent water calls**.
think: I could lose the **evening premium** without losing my title.
I have **ten months** saved, but daytime pay elsewhere may not cover our household bills.
do: Count callbacks and **paid evening hours** each month.
Practise the **required AI tool** on closed outage cases with supervision.
Apply after lost hours for **posted utility work** only with written bill-covering wages and hours; keep shifts until signing an offer.
feel: **Uneasy** about lower wages and an unfamiliar screen.
fieldNote: Uma measures a **whole week of pay**, not the job title on an advertisement.
Her supervised practice requires a **test correction path** before any live reply.

steps.text: Count callbacks and paid evening hours from each monthly roster
Practise required AI replies on closed outage cases with a supervisor
Apply for posted utility work after cuts with written bill-covering wages/hours; keep shifts until signed offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the centre to give us the cut date in writing and name the paid jobs it still needs. I would not say a form can restore a household's water just because it answered the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 could handle the account checks and explanations I am paid for. Robots doing hands-on work arrive around 2031, so the headset does not gain three years. Ten months saved buys time, but nearby centres may all be changing at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a written staffing date now and stop planning a new kitchen floor. In the first year after AGI arrives, if my utility calls end, I'd ask my cousin about a posted paid upholstery apprentice place and apply only if the wage and hours cover our mortgage; I'd take the required class only if the workshop pays the fee and paid study time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, though not without money for a search. I can call my cousin about upholstery, but I cannot make a paid apprenticeship appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why upholstery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Rafi repairs furniture, and I have watched him turn a torn chair into something our family can use again. I know hands-on robots around 2031 could change his workshop too, so I would ask what tasks are still paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your cousin has no opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for another posted utility job with bill-covering wages as a short bridge while keeping the mortgage reserve. I would not ask Rafi to promise a place he has not advertised.

S2.quote: I can call my cousin about upholstery, but I cannot make a paid apprenticeship appear.
say: I would demand a **written cut date** and named paid vacancies.
I would remind colleagues a form cannot **restore water** to a house.
think: I expect AGI to take my **account checks** by 2028.
I know **2031 robots** do not protect the headset, while nearby centres may change together.
do: Ask for a **staffing date** and cancel the kitchen floor purchase now.
Apply for a **posted paid upholstery place** after a cut only if wages and hours cover the mortgage.
Take **required upholstery classes** for a posted paid place only with workshop-funded fees and paid study time; otherwise seek bill-covering utility work.
feel: **Alarmed**, with savings to search but no guaranteed place.
fieldNote: Uma knows **upholstery** through her cousin but refuses to treat family ties as a vacancy.
She asks about **2031 robots** before making the workshop a long-term answer.

steps.text: Cancel the planned kitchen floor purchase to protect savings
Apply for posted paid upholstery after call cuts only if wages and hours cover mortgage
Take required upholstery class only with workshop-paid fees and paid study time
Apply for posted bill-covering utility work if no upholstery vacancy exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets a person learn a trade while still earning, provided there is a real paid opening. I would ask the centre to show how many evening hours remain each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can keep the mortgage current and watch a full day at Rafi's workshop before 2031. AGI will still reach utility calls then, and robots follow around 2034, so a furniture trade may change too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep evening calls and ask Rafi for one paid trial day if his workshop has a place. If a posted paid apprentice opening covers our bills and the workshop pays for required classes on paid time, I'd enrol; in the first year after AGI arrives, if my call hours end, I'd accept only a signed offer with wages and hours that cover our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can make careful visits before deciding. Five years lets me see whether I can stand at a bench all week, not just admire one chair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the trial day tell you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd see the dust, the slow stitching, and whether an apprentice actually earns enough in quiet weeks. A pretty chair may pay less than a full utility rota. I do not want the children to learn that through a missed mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a class yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No; the workshop must pay the fee and my study hours for a named apprentice place. I have saved ten months for household gaps, not for a certificate without a wage.

S3.quote: A pretty chair may pay less than a full utility rota.
say: I would ask for a **paid apprentice opening** before a trade course.
I would track **yearly evening hours** at the centre.
think: I can keep paying the **mortgage** while testing workshop work before 2031.
I see **2034 robots** as a later risk to furniture repair.
do: Keep **evening calls** and try one paid workshop day if a place is available.
Enrol in **required classes** only for a posted bill-covering paid apprenticeship with workshop-funded fees and paid study time.
Accept after 2031 only a **signed apprenticeship offer** whose wages and hours cover the mortgage.
feel: **Worried**, but able to inspect a full workshop day.
fieldNote: Uma asks about **quiet-week apprentice wages**, not only a single successful chair.
The **ten-month reserve** stays for household gaps unless a paid place funds class time.

steps.text: Keep evening utility calls while visiting the workshop
Try one paid upholstery shift if a place is available
Enrol only for bill-covering posted paid apprenticeship with workshop-funded required classes and paid study time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives employers time to publish real paid vacancies. I would rather know the wage for the first apprentice year than hear a speech about new skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I may still owe on the house, though our children will be older. AGI reaches utility calls in 2036 and hands-on robots arrive around 2039, so I will not buy a workshop just because I like Rafi's chairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the utility calls and save a fixed part of each full pay packet. Over the decade I'd check posted upholstery vacancies yearly and take a paid workshop day if one opens; in the first year after AGI arrives, I'd move only if my call hours fall and a signed paid offer covers our mortgage and family hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the far date, steady about this month's work. Ten years before AGI reaches utility calls in 2036 gives me time to check apprentice wages without risking our mortgage today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a written offer with enough paid hours and wages. I would not leave a sure utility shift for an unpaid day at my cousin's bench.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I may learn a different job, but the mortgage and their school routine come first. If I change shifts, Tomas and I will tell them the new pickup plan before it starts.

S4.quote: Ten years before AGI reaches utility calls in 2036 gives me time to check apprentice wages without risking our mortgage today.

fieldNote: Uma gives **mortgage and school pickup** priority over a new craft.

steps.text: Keep utility calls while full paid shifts remain

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it could take the evening calls before a paid upholstery place exists. Written dates, a posted job with wages that cover the mortgage, and workshop-paid classes on paid time would help. Ten months of expenses saved is time to search, not a shop budget.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who calls the household back after an automated notice gives a wrong restoration time. A person at the water company must own a promised restoration time and check the repair report before a family fills buckets again.

headlineQuote: A person at the water company must own a promised restoration time and check the repair report before a family fills buckets again.
portrait: Uma is a **43-year-old experienced agent** on water-service calls, with average skill and secondary schooling.
She earns **higher evening pay**, has ten months saved, a partner, two school-age children, a mortgage, and many nearby centres.
She never uses AI now and keeps a **paper handover book** before trusting a new reply button.
Fast **2028 AGI** threatens call wages; slower timelines allow a paid upholstery trial with written pay and covered classes.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her evening calls before a paid upholstery opening exists.
whatWouldHelp: **Written dates**, posted paid upholstery work, and workshop-funded classes on paid time would help protect the mortgage.
